title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
summary: Automate testing and deployment of your code on every push using GitHub Actions workflows defined in YAML.
objectives: Explain what CI and CD mean and why they matter
Understand triggers, jobs, and steps in a workflow
Run your tests automatically on every push and pull request
Cache dependencies and use a matrix to test multiple versions
Store secrets safely and use them in a deploy step

quiz.why: CI is Continuous Integration: every change is automatically merged, built, and tested so problems surface early.

quiz.q: Where must a GitHub Actions workflow file live in your repository?
options: Anywhere, as long as it ends in .yml
quiz.why: GitHub only runs workflow files placed inside the .github/workflows/ directory.

quiz.q: Which event would you use to run tests when someone opens a pull request?
quiz.why: The pull_request event triggers the workflow when a PR is opened, updated, or reopened.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why should you never paste an API key directly into a workflow file?
quiz.answer: Because the file is committed to the repo and visible to anyone with access; secrets must be stored in encrypted GitHub Secrets and read from the environment.
quiz.why: Hard-coded keys leak the moment the code is shared or made public. Use repository or environment secrets instead.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a job and a step?
quiz.answer: A job is a group of steps that run together on one runner; a step is a single command or action inside a job.
quiz.why: Jobs run in parallel by default on separate runners, while steps inside a job run in order on the same machine.

quiz.q: What does CD usually add on top of CI?
quiz.why: CD extends CI by automatically delivering or deploying the build to staging or production once tests pass.

body_markdown:
## What is CI/CD?

**CI** stands for *Continuous Integration*: every time you push code, it is automatically built and tested so bugs show up within minutes instead of weeks. **CD** stands for *Continuous Delivery* (or *Deployment*): once the tests pass, your code is automatically delivered to staging or shipped to production.

Together, C I C D turns "it works on my machine" into "it provably works, every time, for everyone". GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in tool for this — free for public repos and generous for private ones.

## Anatomy of a workflow

A workflow is a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. It has three core ideas:

- **Triggers** (`on:`) — what events run it, e.g. a push or a pull request.
- **Jobs** — groups of work that run on a fresh virtual machine (a *runner*).
- **Steps** — the individual commands or reusable *actions* inside a job.

```yaml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
```

## Running your tests automatically

The workflow above checks out your code, installs Python, installs your dependencies, then runs `pytest`. If any test fails, the job goes red and GitHub blocks the merge. This is the single highest-value thing CI does for you.

You can speed things up by **caching** dependencies and test many versions at once with a **matrix**:

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
```

## Secrets and deployment (CD)

Never paste an API key into a workflow file — it lives in your repo for anyone to read. Instead store it under **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**, then read it from the environment.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the test report."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

In the workflow, you expose the secret like this so the script can read it:

```yaml
      - name: Smoke test the model
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
        run: python smoke_test.py
```

## Your task

Add a `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to one of your projects that installs dependencies and runs your tests on every push. Confirm it goes green on GitHub.

slides.title: CI/CD with GitHub Actions
slides.sub: Month 5 - Polish, Deploy, Go Public  |  Lesson 3
slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we tackle C I C D with GitHub Actions, one of the most valuable skills you can show an employer. By the end you'll be able to make GitHub automatically test your code on every push and even deploy it for you, all from a single configuration file.

slides.title: What is CI/CD?
bullets: CI: continuous integration — auto build and test.
CD: continuous delivery or deployment.
Catches bugs in minutes, not weeks.
Replaces 'works on my machine'.
slides.narration: Let's start with the words. C I stands for continuous integration: every time you push, your code is automatically built and tested, so bugs surface in minutes. C D stands for continuous delivery or deployment: once tests pass, your code ships automatically. Together they replace the dreaded phrase, it works on my machine.

slides.title: Why GitHub Actions?
bullets: Built right into GitHub — no extra service.
Free for public repos, generous for private.
Defined as code in a YAML file.
Huge marketplace of reusable actions.
slides.narration: GitHub Actions is GitHub's own automation tool, so there's nothing extra to sign up for. It's free for public repositories and generous for private ones. Everything is defined as code in a YAML file that lives beside your project, and there's a huge marketplace of ready-made building blocks you can drop in.

slides.title: Where workflows live
bullets: Put files in .github/workflows/.
Any file ending in .yml or .yaml.
GitHub finds and runs them automatically.
Each file is one workflow.
slides.narration: Workflows live in a special folder: dot github, then workflows. Any file there ending in dot Y M L is picked up automatically. Each file is one workflow. So you might have c i dot Y M L for testing and deploy dot Y M L for shipping. Get that path right or GitHub simply won't see it.

slides.title: Triggers, jobs, steps
bullets: on: which events run the workflow.
jobs: run on fresh virtual machines.
steps: the commands inside a job.
uses: pulls in a reusable action.
slides.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
slides.narration: Three ideas power every workflow. On declares which events trigger it, like a push or a pull request. Jobs are groups of work that each run on a fresh virtual machine called a runner. And steps are the individual commands inside a job. The uses keyword pulls in a reusable action — here, checkout, which grabs your code.

slides.title: Run your tests
bullets: Check out code, set up Python, install deps.
Then run pytest.
A failing test turns the job red.
Red blocks the merge — bugs caught early.
slides.code:
- uses: actions/setup-python@v5
  with:
    python-version: "3.12"
- run: pip install -r requirements.txt
- run: pytest
slides.narration: Here's the heart of it. We set up Python, install our dependencies from requirements dot txt, then run pytest. If any test fails, the job turns red and GitHub blocks the merge. This single automation is the highest value thing C I does, catching broken code before it ever reaches your main branch.

slides.title: Caching and matrix
bullets: Cache dependencies to run faster.
Matrix tests many versions at once.
Each version runs in parallel.
Same steps, less waiting.
slides.code:
strategy:
  matrix:
    python-version: ["3.11", "3.12"]
steps:
  - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
    with:
      python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      cache: pip
slides.narration: Two upgrades make C I faster and stronger. Caching saves your installed dependencies so the next run skips the download. A matrix lets you test several versions at once — here Python three eleven and three twelve — each running in parallel on its own machine, using the very same steps.

slides.title: Secrets, never hard-code
bullets: Never paste keys into the file.
Store them in Settings, Secrets, Actions.
Read them via secrets.NAME.
Expose to a step with env:.
slides.code:
- name: Smoke test
  env:
    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
  run: python smoke_test.py
slides.narration: Anything secret, like an A P I key, must never be pasted into the file — it would live in your repo for anyone to read. Instead store it under settings, secrets and variables, actions. Then reference it with the secrets dot name syntax and expose it to a step through env. GitHub keeps it encrypted and masks it in the logs.

slides.title: Deploying (CD)
bullets: Add a deploy job after tests pass.
needs: makes it wait for test.
Push to staging or production.
Only on the main branch.
slides.code:
deploy:
  needs: test
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - run: ./deploy.sh
slides.narration: For the C D half, we add a deploy job. The needs keyword makes it wait until the test job passes, so we never ship broken code. We also guard it with an if condition, so deployment only happens on the main branch. When all is green, GitHub runs your deploy script for you automatically.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: CI tests every push; CD deploys it.
Workflows live in .github/workflows.
Triggers, jobs, and steps run the show.
Keep secrets out of the file.
Task: add ci.yml that runs your tests.
slides.narration: Let's recap. C I automatically tests every push, and C D deploys once tests pass. Workflows live in dot github slash workflows, built from triggers, jobs, and steps. And secrets always stay out of the file. Your task before the next lesson: add a c i dot Y M L to one of your projects that runs your tests, and watch it go green. Brilliant work — see you next time.
